audiences.communicationIntent: Focus on implementation detail and what other developers must change in their own code. Technical vocabulary is expected. A change is none for contributors only when it touches nothing developers build, test, or call, such as a change to deployment settings alone.

Write for the DBAs who run dbvault against their databases: what touches stored data, schema, credentials, or restore behaviour, what they must check after upgrading, and how to roll back. Name engines (MySQL, PostgreSQL) and versions where they matter. A change is none for DBAs when it touches no stored data, schema, credentials, or restore behaviour and leaves nothing to check after upgrading, such as a console-only, documentation-only, or CI-only change.

Plain language, no jargon and no technical metrics. Say only what the person will notice while using the product. A change is none for end users when they cannot see it: build, CI, dependency, test, and internal changes.

Focus on operational risk, rollback, and what changes in how the product is deployed, configured, or run. Keep concrete numbers and failure modes. Name something to watch after deploying only when the change or the project context names it. A change is none for operators when it changes nothing about deploying, configuring, or running the product, such as a test-only, CI-only, or documentation-only change.

Write for the support team: what customers may notice or ask about, what to tell them, and whether a step is required or only advisable. Plain, precise language. A change is none for support when customers cannot notice it: build, CI, dependency, test, and internal changes.

Write for the dbvault support engineers who answer customers: what customers will notice, what they need to do, and what to tell them. Skip implementation detail. A change is none for support when customers cannot notice it: build, CI, dependency, test, and internal changes.
